Black oreo Allocyttus niger is a deep-water oreosomatid endemic to the temperate Southern Ocean, where it inhabits continental slopes and seamounts at depths exceeding 600 meters. Field surveys indicate that individuals at thermal conditions typical of their subantarctic environment (5.1 °C [T = 5.1 °C]) hatch from the fertilised ovum after an incubation period of 36 days [ab = 36 days], a relatively protracted embryonic duration consistent with the slow developmental rates observed in cold-adapted teleosts. At the moment of chorion rupture, the yolk-sac larva emerges at a minute size, with the wet weight at birth calculated at approximately 0.003 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.003 grams] based on an egg count of 350 eggs per gram. This extremely low neonatal mass reflects the high fecundity characteristic of this species and imposes a stringent energetic challenge during the lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding.

The species attains a maximum recorded body length of 47 centimeters [Li = 47 centimeters], a value derived from extensive survey trawls and representing the asymptotic size achieved by older individuals in the population. In contrast, the total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis, is considerably smaller at 36 centimeters [Lp = 36 centimeters]. Puberty thus occurs well before the ultimate size is reached, a pattern common among iteroparous deep-water fishes that begin allocating resources to reproductive tissue while still investing significantly in somatic growth. The difference of 11 centimeters between these two length thresholds indicates a protracted juvenile phase during which individuals must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to support the metabolic demands of first spawning. Such a delay in reproductive activation is likely linked to the low and unpredictable food availability typical of mesopelagic ecosystems.

Under the same cold thermal regime characterising the species' habitat (5.1 °C [T = 5.1 °C]), the maximum longevity recorded for Allocyttus niger is 100 years [am = 100 years], placing it among the longer-lived teleosts known from the Southern Ocean. This extreme lifespan is consistent with the slow life-history pace typical of deep-water oreosomatids, which experience low natural mortality rates in their thermally stable environment. The combination of a very late age at first reproduction and a century-long reproductive window suggests a life-history strategy heavily reliant on high adult survival rather than on high annual fecundity. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Allocyttus verrucosus indicate similar maximum longevities, reinforcing the idea that extreme longevity is a derived trait within this lineage, presumably shaped by the energetic constraints of deep-water existence.

Female black oreo exhibit a maximum reproductive rate that manifests as a highly fecund spawning strategy, with each gravid individual producing approximately 21,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 21,000 eggs per spawning event]. These spawning events occur roughly three times each year [F_R_i = roughly three times each year] when the fish are maintained at ambient deep-water temperatures of 5.1 °C [T = 5.1 °C], yielding a substantial annual reproductive output. The average daily egg production thus reaches approximately 170 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 170 eggs per day] when the total annual output is averaged across the year. The pelagic eggs are small and laden with yolk, traits that facilitate wide dispersion by oceanic currents but also result in high larval mortality before settlement. This elevated fecundity is characteristic of many demersal, deep-water spawners and offsets the extremely low probability of survival from the yolk-sac larva stage through to the juvenile phase.

Adults of Allocyttus niger eventually reach an ultimate wet weight of approximately 1,650 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,650 grams], a mass that reflects the accumulation of somatic tissue over many decades of slow growth. This body mass, combined with the species' maximum length of 47 centimeters, produces a relatively deep, laterally compressed body form typical of oreosomatids. The weight-length relationship implies a robust condition factor, with individuals investing heavily in both axial musculature and visceral lipid stores that serve as energetic reserves during reproductive bouts. When compared to the minute wet weight at birth of about 0.003 grams [Wwb = about 0.003 grams], the 550,000-fold increase to the ultimate adult mass underscores the extraordinary scope for post-hatching growth. The century-long lifespan (100 years) [am = 100 years] reported for this species is consistent with the profound influence that low temperature (5.1 °C [T = 5.1 °C]) exerts on both developmental and somatic processes in deep-water oreosomatids.
